items.title: sm_75: fewer launches per decode layer: plan wait folded, fused quantize + interleave (bitwise)
items.body:
A verify window launches ~35 dependent kernels per layer on its main stream, and on Turing each dependent graph node costs ~0.8 µs of gap (kernel-node nsys). This folds two pairs that always run back to back into one launch each, writing the same bytes:

- **The plan's host-flag wait folded into its copy**: 143-amdk's `wait_copy_i32_from_mapped`, gfx12-only until now. On CUDA `STRATA_FUSE_WAIT` selects it: `2` = the plan only (the Turing default), `1` = also the CPU rows' `copy_rows_from_mapped_after`, `0` = neither. The rows' version makes every row block of the copy poll the flag over PCIe and was −1.5 % on an RTX 2080 Ti, so it stays opt-in. `STRATA_FUSE_HITS` is unchanged (off on CUDA; measured neutral here).
- **`native_quantize_q8_1_il`**: a projection input's q8_1 blocks and their interleaved copy (`native_q8_1_interleave`) in one kernel. The quantization is `native_quantize_q8_1_kernel`'s; an int of the interleaved copy is four codes gathered from lanes `4p..4p+3` with two shuffles, and the copy's scale is the block's `__low2float(ds)`. Used for the GDN qkv and out-projection inputs and the QSA input and out-projection (`quant_in` in `record_window`); the head keeps its two launches. `STRATA_QIL=0` / `1` forces it off / on; the default is on for sm_75.

Both bitwise: the fused quantize was compared byte for byte with quantize + interleave (both buffers) at 2,560 / 6,144 / 10,240 inputs and 2-4 columns, all-zero blocks included.

## Setup

RTX 2080 Ti 22 GB (sm_75), i7-6700, CUDA 13.0, SM 1650 MHz, 240 W. Flash-Next, canonical Q2_0 pack, `--max-context 524288`, `--serve`, with the other open Turing decode PRs applied.

## Engine (512 new tokens, two runs each, two separate A/Bs)

| A/B 1 | Spanish chat | code | English 32K |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| neither | 90.1 t/s | 107.8 t/s | 80.6 t/s |
| plan wait folded (`STRATA_FUSE_WAIT=2`) | 90.9 | 108.5 | 81.7 |

| A/B 2 | Spanish chat | code | English 32K |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| plan wait folded | 88.3\* | 108.0 | 80.8 |
| + fused quantize | 90.7 | 109.1 | 80.7 |

\* one of the two runs had low draft acceptance (240/337 against ~258/338); the other was 91.4. Small gains (~+1 % and ~+0.5-1 %), but up to three fewer launches per layer in every window, for the same bytes.

Part of the Turing set tracked in #2197.

items.title: qsa_prompt_attn: int8 K/V prefetched in registers and sharing one buffer (Turing / sm_75)
items.body:
## What

Turing (sm_75) only, `--kv int8` only: the prompt attention kernel that Turing runs (v1, `qsa_prompt_attn.cu`) gets
faster with the same output bits. Other GPUs and other KV modes run the same code as before.

## Why

On Turing the v1 kernel used 37.9 KB of shared memory per 128-thread block, so only one block fit on an SM (4 warps,
12.5 % of what an SM can hold). Each 32-cell chunk also loaded its scattered K and V rows only after the previous
chunk had finished. Nsight Compute on a CMP 50HX (TU102, RTX 2080 Ti class) showed `long_scoreboard` (waiting on
global loads) as the top stall.

## Change

1. **The next chunk's int8 K/V rows and scales go into registers while the current chunk computes**, then are stored
   where the old gather stored them. (sm_80+ uses `cp.async` for this; Turing does not have it.)
2. **K and V share one shared-memory buffer.** K is read only by the scores and V only by `p·v`, so V is written over
   K after the scores' barrier; the softmax's barrier keeps it before `p·v`. 37.9 -> 29.2 KB per block: **two blocks
   per SM** instead of one.

The same bytes land in the same places and the arithmetic is unchanged, so the results are bitwise the same.

`qsa_prompt_attn_parity` now also prints a checksum of the new kernel's output, so two builds can be compared bit
for bit.

## Measured

CMP 50HX (sm_75, unlocked to RTX 2080 speed, 20 GB), CUDA 13.3, GCC 14.2.

`qsa_prompt_attn_parity`, int8, 2,048 queries:

| context | before | after | change |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 40K | 21.45 ms | 12.91 ms | -40 % |
| 140K | 21.94 ms | 13.31 ms | -39 % |

All output checksums (int8 and fp16, at 4K / 40K / 140K) match the old kernel.

Whole engine: Flash-Next IQ3_XXS, 2x CMP 50HX with `--layer-split auto`, 2x Xeon E5-2670 v2. A coding-agent session
grew from 34K to 190K tokens over 36 turns (+~4.4K tokens per turn, greedy, fresh server per run). The text of all 36
turns was identical to the old build. Incremental prompt read time went down 3.5 % (median per-turn ratio 0.965), and
decode did not change.

Note: these numbers were measured on a fork based on 0.1.38. The patch applies to current `main` without changes;
re-measuring on 0.1.41 is still to do.

## How to check

On an sm_75 card, before and after:

```
qsa_prompt_attn_parity 40000 2048
qsa_prompt_attn_parity 140000 2048
```

The `new output checksum` lines should be equal and the time per chunk lower.

items.title: qsa_select: the FP32 tiled block scores below sm_80 (PR #1091) on by default; STRATA_SELECT_SIMT=0 keeps the warp kernel
items.body:
## Title
Issue: none (a default change below sm_80, with the numbers).

## Summary
#1091 (konijiwa110) added the FP32 tiled QSA block-scores kernel for the prompt path below sm_80 and it was merged
**opt-in** (`STRATA_SELECT_SIMT=1`). This turns it **on by default** on compute capability < 8.0; `STRATA_SELECT_SIMT=0`
keeps the warp kernel. sm_80 and newer keep their TF32 tensor-core kernel; HIP is untouched.

## Why
On Turing the warp kernel runs at ~1 TFLOPS against ~6.9 for the tiled one, and the QSA block scores are a visible
share of a long prompt. #1091 measured +22% at 128K and +44% at 248K prompt speed on an RTX 2080 Ti; here, with the
two sm_75 changes of the same series, a 131K prompt on the 2080 Ti stage went from 100 s to 75 s. The ready-made
engine is what most Turing users run, and they do not read the environment table.

## What changed
`src/kernels/cuda/qsa_select.cu` (`qsa_block_scores_tc`: the `simt` default), `include/strata/kernels/qsa_select.hpp`
(the comment), `src/prefill/prefill.cpp` (the log line says which kernel ran).

## Bit for bit
No: the tiled kernel sums in another order than the warp kernel, as the opt-in already did. The prompt's selection
can differ at the rounding level.

## Measurements
RTX 2080 Ti 22 GB + RTX 3060 12 GB, Windows 11, CUDA 12.6, layer split (the 2080 Ti holds layers 16-47), Qwen3.8
IQ3_XXS: 131K prompt 100 s -> 75 s together with the 16-byte dequant and hc16 (separate PRs). TITAN RTX, #1981: the
community report ran with the switch on.

Built and started on v0.1.43 (RTX 2080 Ti + RTX 3060 layer split, Windows): the engine serves as before, same answer. The prompt-time figures come from this fork's daily build, where the three Turing prefill changes have run together since 0.1.40.

Part of a series from a public patch registry (`stack/` in the fork imanu86/Strata-2080Ti), see #2073.

items.title: sm_75: the v2 prompt attention in one stage, three blocks per SM (bitwise, attention 1.66x; stacked on #2092)
items.body:
Stacked on #2092 (the Turing v2 prompt attention, `STRATA_PA_V2T=1`): its first commit is #2092's.

With register staging, #2092's v2 keeps the next chunk's K/V pieces in registers until the current chunk's p·v is done, so its second shared-memory stage buys nothing on Turing - but `Smem2` is 45.6 KB and a Turing SM has 64 KB: one 4-warp block per SM, one warp per scheduler, every latency exposed. ncu on a 130K chunk: 12.5 % warps active, the tensor pipe at 8 %.

Below sm_80 the kernel now takes `Smem2T`: one K/V stage, and no separate q·k partials (`part`, 8.4 KB). The partials of cell group `nt` (8 cells, 16 rows) are exactly 512 bytes, and the cells they come from occupy bytes `[512 nt, 512 nt + 512)` of the warp's own K slice (the swizzle stays inside a cell's 64 bytes), read by then - so after a `__syncwarp` each group's partials overwrite its own cells. The softmax reads them across warps after the same `__syncthreads` as before, and the next chunk's `store_stage` comes after the second one, as before. 19.7 KB a block: three per SM (168 registers fit three). Same arithmetic, same order: the same bits.

The second commit adds `tests/cuda/pa_bench.cpp`, which replays a recorded selection (`STRATA_QSA_DUMP` gets `STRATA_QSA_DUMP_LAYER=i` and `STRATA_QSA_DUMP_STEPS=1`), random q and int8 K/V, and prints the median time and an output hash.

## Setup

RTX 2080 Ti 22 GB (sm_75), i7-6700, CUDA 13.0, SM 1650 MHz, 240 W; `v0.1.43` + #2092. Q2_0, `--prefill auto:16384`, `STRATA_PA_V2T=1`.

items.title: prefill: the fused int8 prompt experts on Turing (sm_75), opt-in (+9 % prefill on RTX 2080 Ti)
items.body:
On Turing the prompt path's experts always go through llama.cpp's MMQ: the fused int8 kernels (`moe_fused.cu` for the Strata Q2_0 pack, `moe_fused_iq.cu`'s `native_kernel` for the native packs, #136) need sm_80. On an RTX 2080 Ti MMQ's Q2_0 kernel runs at ~20-30 TOPS (255 registers with spills, one CTA per SM) and is the largest single cost of a long prompt read.

This ports both to sm_75, opt-in on top of `STRATA_PF_FUSED=1` with `STRATA_PF_FUSED_SM75=1`:

- `cp.async` → plain 16-byte copies (the barriers around them stay), `prefetch.global.L2` kept;
- `mma` m16n8k32 / m16n8k16 with s8 operands → four / two `m8n8k16` (rows g / g + 8 by k 0-15 / 16-31). The int32 sums are exact in any order, so `d` is what the sm_80 instruction gives; MAGIC is passed as the C operand of each pair's first `m8n8k16`;
- two activation stages below sm_80 (64 KB of shared memory per SM), `smem_bytes` / the launch / the occupancy query take the device's depth (`host_astages()`);
- `native_kernel` takes **Q2_0 gate/up** (64-value blocks: a block per stage, as the down rows already read theirs), so the canonical Q2_0 pack (Q2_0 / Q2_0 in every layer) runs fused. `gu_covered()` lists Q2_0 on CUDA;
- on Turing only that pair is set up (`DevInfo::t75`: `native_supported` answers false for the others, which keep MMQ);
- Turing, Q2_0 only (`T75_DEV`): a stage's two 32-value halves share the block's `d`, so a row's dot is `d (dx_0 dot_0 + dx_1 dot_1)` - 11 % fewer instructions (the kernel is bound by its FP32 epilogue on Turing, not the tensor pipe). sm_80+ keeps its code and bits.

`prefill_fused_iq_test` gets the Q2_0 / Q2_0 pair, and skips the pairs a Turing card does not set up instead of failing.

## Setup

RTX 2080 Ti 22 GB (sm_75), i7-6700, CUDA 13.0, SM 1650 MHz, 240 W; `v0.1.43`. Canonical Q2_0 pack, `--prefill auto:16384`, `STRATA_BF16_TC=1`, `STRATA_SELECT_SIMT=2`.

## Kernels (`prefill_fused_iq_test --only="Q2_0 / Q2_0"`, one layer, 512 experts, top 10)

| tokens | MMQ path | fused | |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2,048 | 12.99 ms | 6.61 ms | 1.96× |
| 8,192 | 30.75 ms | 21.18 ms\* | 1.45× |
| 16,384 | 55.02 ms | 37.15 ms | 1.48× |

\* before the Q2_0 epilogue change. Fused vs MMQ rel RMS 1.6e-5 - 2.7e-5; both 1.09e-2 against the FP32 reference (the int8 activations' own error). `prefill_fused_moe_test` (Strata pack) passes too: 5.29 ms fused vs MMQ 3.67×, rel RMS 6.7e-5.

## Engine

98K prompt (16K chunks, two runs each, deterministic run to run): 58.3 → 53.3 s (+9.4 %). 4K: 3.63 → 3.54 s.

Accuracy in the engine: layer 0 of a 32K prompt (identical input on both paths), every one of the 163,840 (token, expert) rows of the expert output against MMQ's: median rel 1.6e-7, p99.9 2.6e-3, max 7.6e-3 (the rows where H's int8 rounding falls the other way); against the FP16 expert path (`STRATA_PREFILL_MMQ=0`) MMQ and fused have the same error (median 1.08e-2).

Teacher-forced, as in #655 / #2071 (the first P tokens through the prompt path, the next 2,048 through the verify windows, `STRATA_LOGPOS_TOPK=20`):

| P | KL (MMQ ‖ fused) | KL (FP16 ‖ MMQ) | perplexity FP16 / MMQ / fused |
|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 16,384 | 0.0101 | 0.0090 | 7.308 / 7.255 / 7.501 |
| 32,768 | 0.0226 | 0.0110 | 4.561 / 4.557 / 4.354 |
| 65,536 | 0.0186 | 0.0262 | 4.110 / 4.096 / 4.122 |

The perplexity moves either way (+3.4 %, −4.5 %, +0.6 %) - trajectory noise: the QSA selection is discrete, so any change of the prompt path's rounding gives KLs of this size (enabling only one layer's fused experts already moves the first logit by KL ~1e-3, as much as the FP16 path in every layer). The verify phase's time over the same 2,048 tokens: MMQ 42.36 s, fused 42.28 s.

The server here will run with `STRATA_PF_FUSED=1 STRATA_PF_FUSED_SM75=1`.

items.title: verify: STRATA_NO_PCIE_GROUP=1 drops the empty PCIe-share stage with --pcie-frac 0
items.body:
With `--pcie-frac 0` the pool never plans PCIe experts, yet every layer of a verify window still runs the PCIe-share stage over zero groups: the flag B wait, `fetch_blobs` + `rebase_ptrs` (staging mode 2) and the grouped gate/up, SwiGLU and down launches with `kPcieGroupRows` rows that find nothing to do. Six dependent kernels, ~18 µs a layer on an RTX 2080 Ti (kernel-node nsys), ~0.86 ms of a ~25 ms window.

`STRATA_NO_PCIE_GROUP=1` records the window graph without that stage. It is opt-in and only valid with `--pcie-frac 0` (the graphs are captured once, and the share can otherwise be refined at run time): if the pool ever publishes a plan with PCIe experts, the host loop stops the engine with a message (`STRATA_NO_PCIE_GROUP=1 needs --pcie-frac 0 (layer L planned N PCIe experts)`) after releasing the GPU's waits, instead of letting the GPU skip experts. I checked that path by starting the engine without `--pcie-frac 0`: it stops at the first window that plans a PCIe expert.

On this card, with the expert cache warm (~96-97 % VRAM hits in decode), the CPU takes the few misses the PCIe share would have taken without a measurable loss: `--pcie-frac 0` alone was neutral (Spanish 86.9 vs 87.8 t/s, code 106.3 vs 106.1, 32K 78.2 vs 78.4 - within the run-to-run spread).

## Setup

RTX 2080 Ti 22 GB (sm_75), i7-6700 (4 cores), 56 GB DDR4-2133, PCIe 3.0 x16, CUDA 13.0, SM 1650 MHz, 240 W. Flash-Next, canonical Q2_0 pack, `--resident-experts`, `--max-context 524288`, `--serve`, with the other open Turing decode PRs applied.

## Engine (512 new tokens, two runs each)

| | `--pcie-frac` auto | `--pcie-frac 0` + `STRATA_NO_PCIE_GROUP=1` | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Spanish chat (57-token prompt) | 87.8 t/s | 89.8 t/s | +2.3 % |
| code | 106.1 | 108.4 | +2.2 % |
| English, 32K | 78.4 | 80.1 | +2.2 % |
| English, 128K | 75.0 | 76.8 | +2.4 % |
| English, 389,560 tokens | 74.7 | 75.1 | +0.6 % |

The prompt reads are unchanged (32K 17.6 s, 390K 223.6 s).

A follow-up could make this automatic when `--pcie-frac 0` is given (no env), if you prefer that.

items.title: sm_75: Q2_0 matvec with one warp per four rows (bitwise)
items.body:
On Turing the Q2_0 matvec of the decode windows is far from the card's bandwidth: the QSA layers' `attn_q` (2560 → 12288, Q2_0 in the canonical pack) takes 80 µs at three columns, ~110 GB/s on an RTX 2080 Ti. The exact layout gives each row four warps and half a 64-value block per thread, then a cross-warp reduction; at the engine's 2,560 inputs a row has 40 blocks, so 48 of the 128 threads have no chunk and the reduction is most of the kernel.

`q2_0_warp_rows_kernel` gives a warp four rows. Lane `l` runs the chunks of the exact kernel's threads `l`, `32 + l`, `64 + l` and `96 + l`, in their loop order, adds the four sums the way warp 0 adds the other warps' partials, then the same `warp_sum`. Every output is bit for bit `native_q2_0_mmvq_kernel`'s (one column) and `launch_multi`'s exact layout (two to four columns); the upstream (non-exact) layout keeps its kernel.

Default on sm_75 only (the only card I can measure); `STRATA_Q2_WARP=0` keeps the old kernels, `=1` takes this one on any CUDA card.

## Setup

RTX 2080 Ti 22 GB (sm_75), i7-6700, CUDA 13.0, SM 1650 MHz, 240 W. Flash-Next, canonical Q2_0 pack, `--max-context 524288`, `--serve`.

## Kernel (2560 × 12288, cold weights: six copies in rotation, 300 calls)

| columns | exact layout | warp rows | |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 36.6 µs | 24.8 µs | 1.48× |
| 2 | 59.8 µs | 31.4 µs | 1.90× |
| 3 | 68.3 µs | 31.3 µs | 2.18× |
| 4 | 88.4 µs | 36.6 µs | 2.42× |

The outputs are compared with `memcmp` against the engine's own launch for every column count: identical. One and two rows per warp, and eight warps per block, were measured too; four rows and four warps was best.

## Engine

Together with the QSA attention change of #2220 (both bitwise, measured as one step), 512 new tokens, two runs each: Spanish chat 86.0 → 87.8 t/s, code 103.1 → 106.1, English at 32K 75.3 → 78.4. The same kernel also serves the shared expert's Q2_0 gate/up on its side stream.

items.title: sm_75: Turing tables for the decode matvecs and the grouped experts (bitwise, decode +6 %)
items.body:
Two Turing-only defaults, both bitwise equal to what RTX 20 runs today, both with a switch to turn them off. Measured on an RTX 2080 Ti; I have no other sm_75 card to check them on.

1. **`kIlRows_75`** (`native_mmvq.cu`): the interleaved small-batch matvec kernels with their own table, as Volta and Pascal have. The 2-6 column dense projections of a verify window ran the plain multi-column kernels, which on Turing are bound by `dp4a` throughput from 2 columns on. `STRATA_SM75_IL=0` keeps the plain kernels. No one-column table: the engine's dedicated single-column kernels sum in another order, for a 0.5 % gain.
2. **Expert layout mode 4 on sm_75** (`iq_kernels.cu`, `exp_mode()`): the AMD layouts already build for CUDA; mode 4 is bitwise equal to mode 0 and faster for the window's usual 1-2 entries per expert. items.title: sm_75: the v2 int8 prompt attention with register staging instead of cp.async (STRATA_PA_V2T=1)
items.body:
On Turing the int8-KV prompt attention runs v1, because v2 (`prompt_attn_i8_kernel`) stages each warp's K/V slices with `cp.async`, which does not exist before sm_80. v1 keeps one 4-warp CTA per SM (37 KB of shared memory) and gathers a chunk, waits, computes; the attention is ~18 % of a 130K prompt read on an RTX 2080 Ti.

Here, below sm_80, v2's `issue()` loads the warp's next pieces into registers (4 + 4 `uint4` a lane) and `store_stage()` writes them into the warp's other stage after the current chunk's p·v, where v2 already stores the next chunk's scales - the same bytes in the same places as the cp.async pipeline; each warp only touches its own stages, so `__syncwarp` suffices as before. The MMAs are the m16n8k8 pairs v1 already uses on Turing. Opt-in (`STRATA_PA_V2T=1`): another summation order than v1, like v2 against v1 on sm_80.

## Setup

RTX 2080 Ti 22 GB (sm_75), i7-6700, CUDA 13.0, driver 595, SM 1650 MHz, 240 W; `v0.1.43`. Model Q2_0, `--resident-experts`, `--max-context 524288`, `--kv int8 --kv-resident 32768`, `STRATA_BF16_TC=1`, `STRATA_SELECT_SIMT=2`.

## `qsa_prompt_attn_parity` (int8 KV), ms per chunk and error against FP64

| context × queries | v1 | v2 (register staged) | error vs FP64, v1 / v2 (output scale) |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 32K × 1024 | 12.98 | 7.63 | 4.3e-6 / 3.7e-6 (3.7) |

items.title: sm_75: a hyper-connection up kernel for 3+ tokens and the staged down kernel in token pairs (bitwise)
items.body:
The hyper-connection read is ~19 % of an RTX 2080 Ti's decode GPU time (96 reads per window, 13 MB of BF16 weights each). Two Turing-only changes, both bitwise equal to the kernels they replace (`gr_parity`, `gr_multi_parity`, and the same `fused_gr_bench` hashes):

1. **`gr_up75_kernel`** for 3+ tokens: two batches of 4 rows of `w_up` loaded before the dots (was: one row's load after the previous row's epilogue; ncu showed ~9k of a warp's ~22k cycles waiting on memory), each token's activations read from shared memory once per batch, the 4 xor reductions interleaved, and the rows' last 8 chunks held 4 rows to a `uint4` and shuffled to their lane. Every row's lane sums, xor tree and epilogue are `gr_up_multi_kernel`'s. At 1-2 tokens `gr_up_multi_kernel` is as fast or faster, so it stays there. `STRATA_GR_UP75=0` turns it off.
2. **The staged down kernel takes a token group from `blockIdx.y`**: on sm_75 a launch of 4 or 6 tokens runs as pairs, more blocks for the 41-block grid; every (row, token) is still summed by one warp exactly as before. `STRATA_GR_DOWN_TG=n` forces groups of n (0 = off). One token per group is slower at every T (the weights are read from L2 once per group), so only pairs.

items.title: sm_75: QSA decode attention for INT8 KV off the shared-memory pipe (bitwise)
items.body:
The decode attention over the QSA selection (`attn_chunk_kernel<1>`, INT8 pools) saturates the SM's shared-memory pipe on Turing. Its time grew linearly with the queries while the SMs were half empty: per cell, every warp reads two 16-byte slices of each of the 12 query heads from shared memory (a two-way bank conflict at `lane * 8`) and runs 12 `warp_sum`s, 60 shuffles; the value loop then reads the 12 probabilities of a cell as 12 scalar loads. Loading the K/V codes earlier (software prefetch) changed nothing, so it is not memory latency.

`attn_chunk_q8_v3_kernel` does the same operations in the same order:

- the lane's slice of the 12 heads (8 dimensions each) is read from shared memory once, into registers;
- the 12 lane sums are reduced with `reduce12_gfx906` (16 shuffles; every sum is `warp_sum`'s pairs, as its comment says);
- the probabilities are stored cell-major, so the value loop reads a cell's 12 as three 16-byte broadcasts.

The chunk partials and the merged output are bit for bit the default kernel's. It is used by both entry points (`qsa_decode_attn_batch`, `qsa_decode_attn_step`), so the MTP drafter's attention gets it too. Default on sm_75 only; `STRATA_ATTN_V3=0` keeps the default kernel, `=1` takes this one on any CUDA card. Lane-cell scoring (`STRATA_ATTN_LANECELL=1`) keeps its path.

## Setup

RTX 2080 Ti 22 GB (sm_75), i7-6700, CUDA 13.0, SM 1650 MHz, 240 W. Flash-Next, canonical Q2_0 pack, `--kv int8`, `--max-context 524288`, `--serve`.

## Kernel (chunk kernel + merge, synthetic INT8 pools, permuted page table, 200 calls)

| selected cells | queries | default | v3 | |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2,051 | 1 | 51.6 µs | 34.5 µs | 1.50× |
| 2,051 | 2 | 78.5 µs | 41.0 µs | 1.91× |
| 2,051 | 3 | 110.0 µs | 73.0 µs | 1.51× |
| 2,051 | 4 | 145.6 µs | 84.9 µs | 1.71× |
| 600 | 1 | 45.9 µs | 28.6 µs | 1.60× |
| 600 | 2 | 74.6 µs | 32.8 µs | 2.27× |
| 600 | 3 | 105.5 µs | 33.5 µs | 3.15× |
| 600 | 4 | 136.9 µs | 33.3 µs | 4.11× |

Partials and outputs compared with `memcmp` against the default kernel in every case: identical. With the swizzle and `reduce12` alone (the gfx906 variants, also bitwise on CUDA) the 2,051-cell / 3-query case is 78 µs; the register copy of the query is what takes it to 73 µs, and further at fewer cells. At 2,051 cells and 3-4 queries the registers allow two blocks per SM (198-264 blocks: two waves); forcing three spills.

`qsa_prompt_attn_parity` reports the same errors with `STRATA_ATTN_V3=0` and `1` (its reference is this decode kernel: int8 32K / 2,048 queries 71.5 → 36.0 ms per chunk).

## Engine

Together with the Q2_0 matvec change of #2221 (both bitwise, measured as one step), 512 new tokens, two runs each: Spanish chat 86.0 → 87.8 t/s, code 103.1 → 106.1, English at 32K 75.3 → 78.4.

Part of the Turing set tracked in #2197.

items.title: prefill: scope each split-stage loan estimate to its device
items.body:
A layer-split prompt borrows buffers from each stage's expert cache. This makes the `part_slots` estimate run under `OnDevice(p.dev)`, matching the device scope used by `Prefill::init` and the other prompt-buffer estimates. When initialization fails inside a borrowed region, the diagnostic also reports that region's capacity.

This is a small consistency change, not a demonstrated fix for a failure in current upstream. At upstream `d5ea7133741e67743c0e886bb426c0ce8d69cf6c`, CUDA `prompt_f16()` is always false and the HIP setting is process-wide, so these devices currently produce the same count. The added scope makes the existing contract explicit before device-specific buffers are introduced.

The motivating failure occurred in our fork, which has extra Turing-only prompt buffers: RTX 3060 as the first stage and RTX 2080 Ti as the last stage, on Windows. The later stage's loan was undercounted even though free VRAM remained. Those fork-specific buffers are not part of this PR, and their successful run is not validation of this exact upstream branch.

Validation and scope:

- Branch `pr/split-prompt-borrow`, head `4f9f14892da9e9d401dd7f6360e71b311912858a`, one commit over `82f46a8c8f475f001ad76d92f58f4a4f8ffb0253`.
- `git diff --check 82f46a8..HEAD` passes. Read-only inspection against current upstream confirms neither addition is present there.
- No fresh build or GPU run of this exact branch was performed for publication. CUDA/HIP compilation and a long-prompt layer-split regression remain pending.
- No numerical kernel changes, new option, or speed claim. `OnDevice` restores the previous device when the count ends.

Suggested validation is to compare prompt loan sizes and successful prompt ingestion before/after on an ordinary layer split. Reproducing the original undercount requires device-specific allocation differences, which current upstream does not have.

items.title: Port Maya v1.0.14 NVIDIA GLM updates to Strata v0.1.41
items.body:
## Summary

Port compatible NVIDIA GLM updates from Project Maya `cfd2f45b506be6c02d715e3198b3ff9719de25fc` (v1.0.4) through `327cfa60d46f9d8eea33a1b38e76284646fbad86` (v1.0.14), integrated with Strata 0.1.41 main `fb58e0dbc8399662c0e47c76578c6e878b14f6cf`.

- GLM windowed MoE prefill, CPU/PCIe balancing, 3% RAM landing buffers with a 12–96 automatic range, GPU-sized chunks and next-layer read-ahead.
- Turing register WMMA and Ampere mma.sync attention, typed dense GEMV and contiguous CPU expert work pieces. Preserve the local synthetic Q4_0 path, latent sizing/alignment, slow diagnostic path and safe F32 fallback.
- Layer splits for up to 16 visible NVIDIA GPUs with input validation before planning. Add opt-in SSD text conversation slots, isolated per engine process and bounded by a disk budget/free-space reserve.
- Native GLM tool calls, streamed typed arguments, forced tool choice, and GLM tokenizer metadata at server startup. Reuse Strata 0.1.41 request hardening, API formats, dashboard and Qwen default.
- Explicit Maya-M/GSQ-RCO-3.5bit model choices alongside the existing Maya-S v2 default, immutable Hub revisions and verified SHA-256 manifests. GSQ has no MTP weights. Keep model downloads behind explicit consent.
- Opt-in GLM CPU-lane calibration through the existing installer and settings store. No measurement run with a model in this checkout.

### Conflict resolution and PR scope

Merge commits `ff9f6b8832b4d12aba40f8553204d120b7a3cc05` (PR #1420) and `0db33ad` resolve conflicts against official main without rewriting published history. Resolutions preserve the upstream CUDA toolkit discovery, baseline-ISA native-expert predicates and tokenizer piece cache together with the GLM adaptations.

This draft remains cumulative while #1420 is unmerged. The latest Maya update itself is [the incremental comparison](https://github.com/apr3ndi5/Strata/compare/0db33ad...cd297de8eaf60aea26011f50e5f4799d34d2cd42). No maintainer PR was merged or closed.

### Compatibility limits

This is a selective port, not a copy of the entire Maya fork. GLM continues to target native Linux/NVIDIA and experimental native Windows x64/NVIDIA; WSL, AMD/HIP and Intel remain rejected. Maya's new AMD extension requires its different HIP intrinsics/WMMA headers, tuning tables and GLM GEMM linkage, so it is not enabled here. The extra segment tokenizer cache, Maya launcher and benchmark command are not copied; Strata's existing piece cache, installer and diagnostics are retained.

No performance measurements from Maya are presented as measurements of this Strata integration. Full-model inference remains unverified. Installed models, configs and environments were preserved; MIT/OFL notices remain.

## Fresh validation — 2026-10-08

These results were run for this update, separately from previous PR results, on Windows with Python 3.10.5 and MSVC 19.51 / Visual Studio 2026:

- **1,116 distinct Python cases: 1,106 passed, 10 skipped**: full `serve` discovery 605 (596 passed/9 skipped), all `tools/test_setup_*.py` unittest modules 444 passed, additional pack/oracle/tokenizer/calibration modules 67 (66 passed/1 skipped). Repeated focused runs are not counted twice.
- The first full server run found an existing short-name/long-name Windows path comparison in the slots test. Canonicalizing the compared path fixed the expectation, and the final full run passed.
- **Five C++ CPU tests passed**: conversation cache, conversation memory, native split, prefill memory (19 checks) and GLM device-list parsing (12 checks).
- New Q2_K/Q3_K AVX-512 kernel and synthetic test compiled with MSVC. Arithmetic was explicitly skipped because this CPU lacks AVX-512.
- Synthetic Q4_0 fixture generated and packed on CPU: 184 tensors, 15 routed expert tensors, five disk-backed MoE layers. This is fixture/packing verification, not inference.
- CPU image encoder built; existing vendor MSBuild duplicate-source warning remains. Python/JavaScript syntax and Git whitespace checks passed.
- CMake rejected GLM with SYCL and without CUDA. Native Windows GLM configuration reached CUDA discovery and stopped at `No CUDA toolset found`.

Reproduce the Python tools group with `python -m unittest tools.test_glm_pack tools.test_glm_oracle tools.test_iq_pack tools.test_calibrate tools.test_calibrate_glm tools.test_strata_tokenizer`; server group with `python -m unittest discover -s serve -t .`. Installer modules were collected from `tools/test_setup_*.py` and loaded with `unittest.defaultTestLoader.loadTestsFromNames`.

### Pending hardware checks

CUDA compilation/device linking; F32/WMMA/Turing-register/Ampere-mma attention parity; synthetic Q4_0 multichunk SSD prefill parity; real pinned-allocation cleanup; SSD slot round-trips; multiple-GPU pipelines; model calibration; full-model text/image/MTP quality and performance. The CPU kernel arithmetic also needs AVX-512 hardware. This checkout has no CUDA toolkit; VS 2026 does not meet the recommended CUDA 12.8/VS 2022 combination. The PR remains a draft.

No weights were downloaded and no production engine/server started. Mock server tests and generated local fixtures were used.

Final update commit: `cd297de8eaf60aea26011f50e5f4799d34d2cd42`.

## What was tested

generated tokens by request time. Every prompt is byte-fresh with a nonce; **`reused 0` on all
twelve sweep runs**.

| Test | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Fresh prompt / decode, 3 runs each | 4K: **728.4** / **61.5** tok/s · 32K: **1,012.8** / **53.1** · 128K: **896.5** / **53.2** |

1. **The measurement agent shared the engine.** This box serves the agent that ran the scripts

2. **Warm expert cache for the main sweep.** All nine sweep runs share one long-lived session.
   Run 1 of each length is clearly slower (32K: 37.7 tok/s at 92.6% hit) than runs 2-3 (55.6
   median at ~98% hit); both are reported separately in the README.
3. **The cold arm is a cold *engine*, not a cold boot.** `POST /unload` + `POST /load` restarts

   page cache, so file reads are warm. 37 s of the 65.7 s is re-creating the page-locked,

  `--vram-reserve-mib` sweep say the auto sizer is leaving too little on a 48 GB card?
- **A freshly restarted engine beat the first run inside the long session.** First touch after

  after a clean profile-driven start?

`README.md` in the folder lists every command, the exact engine arguments, and the field names
and units of each JSON file. Folder is 448 KB — no model files, no packs, no API keys, and the
logs contain token counts and timings only, no prompt or answer text.

items.title: sm_75: the prompt path's top-k with one full read of the scores (identical ids)
items.body:
**Builds on #2072** (it sits next to that PR's split top-k in `qsa_select.cu`); the first commit here is #2072's, the second is this one.

Past ~115K cells the prompt path's top-k is DRAM traffic on Turing: `block_topk_wide_kernel` reads a query's scores six times (four radix passes, a count, the emit), 400 KB a query at 400K, 256 queries a call.

`block_topk_sample_kernel` reads them once:
1. a bound LB: the KS-th largest key among every 32nd block (KS = 2 × the selection's blocks / 32 + 16);
2. one read of all blocks, keeping those with key ≥ LB in shared memory;
3. when those hold at least `width` cells, the width-th largest cell key (block_topk_kernel's threshold) is ≥ LB, so every block at or above the threshold is a candidate: the threshold, `above` and the tie budget computed over the candidates with block_topk_kernel's rule are the reference's, and the candidates sorted by block (bitonic) emit the reference's cells in its order;
4. otherwise (too few cells above LB, or more than 4,096 candidates) the query is flagged and `block_topk_wide_kernel<true>` runs it - the all-equal-scores case of the parity test takes that path.

Used for prompt calls above 28,672 active blocks (below, the wide kernel is as fast); `STRATA_TOPK_SAMPLE=0` keeps the wide kernel.

## Setup

RTX 2080 Ti 22 GB (sm_75), i7-6700, CUDA 13.0, driver 595, SM 1650 MHz, 240 W; `v0.1.43` + #2072, `-DSTRATA_BUILD_TESTS=ON`. Model Q2_0, `--max-context 524288`, `--kv int8 --kv-resident 32768`, `STRATA_SELECT_SIMT=2` (#2071).

## `qsa_topk_parity CTX 256 20 524288 1` (a prompt call), dispatched time

| context | wide | sample |
|---|---:|---:|
| 98K | 0.397 ms | 0.396 (wide: below the bound) |
| 131K | 0.513 | 0.452 |
| 262K | 0.952 | 0.589 |
| 400K | 1.476 | 0.706 |
| 520K | 1.840 | 0.787 |

`qsa_topk_parity --selftest`: PASS (continuous, 64-level and equal scores; identical ids). `qsa_topk_active_parity` (`STRATA_TOPK_ACTIVE_ANY=1`): 20 cases, identical.

First logits after a 196K prompt: bitwise identical to the run without it (`STRATA_DUMP_FIRST_LOGITS`). The gain sits at depth: with this, #2071 and #2091 and #2092, appending 16K tokens to a 390K conversation (`--serve`) went 15.9 → 12.9 s here.

items.title: strata-q36 on Volta: K-quant prompt experts on a register-fragment tensor-core kernel - prompt +22-25% on a V100, same tokens
items.body:
On a Volta GPU, strata-q36's prompt-path MoE experts in Q4_K / Q5_K / Q6_K now use a new FP16 tensor-core kernel (`moe_tc_kq`) instead of MMQ's dp4a path. This covers the gate/up and down products of a prompt chunk.

**How it works**
- A block handles 64 routed rows against 128 weight rows, with 8 warps.
- In each warp, the four `mma.m8n8k4` quad pairs each take a 32-value chunk of a 128-value k step.
- Each lane decodes its row's 32 values straight into A fragments in registers, with the same arithmetic as ggml's `dequantize_row_q*_K`. Weights are never staged in shared memory.
- The q8_1 activations MMQ already produces (DS4 for Q4_K/Q5_K, D4 for Q6_K) are staged as FP16 in shared memory, double-buffered, with the next step's loads in flight under the current step's products.
- The four chunks' partial sums are added with shuffles. Accumulation is FP32.

**Scope**
- Used only when the device is sm_70. Turing and newer already run MMQ on int8 tensor cores.
- `STRATA_PREFILL_TCKQ=0` keeps MMQ.
- The source is compiled only when `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES` includes 70 (or `native`/`all`). It is about 140 KB of device code, so default builds (`120`) are unchanged. Outside that build the header's inline no-ops leave the call site free of `#ifdef`s.

**Measured** on one Tesla V100 PCIe 32 GB with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MTP-UD-Q4_K_M. The build is this branch on main 296b59d2 with `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=70 -DSTRATA_MMQ_KQUANTS=ON`. Each run is `strata-q36 --bench-pp` (`--max-context 131072`), plus a 16K-token greedy generation compared by md5. Two cooled rounds, alternating the two settings:

| | `STRATA_PREFILL_TCKQ=0` (MMQ) | default (this kernel) |
|---|---:|---:|
| pp512 | 1,685.9 / 1,684.4 | **2,109.0 / 2,109.3** (+25%) |
| pp16384 | 1,518.8 / 1,518.3 | **1,854.6 / 1,854.2** (+22%) |
| MTP2 pp512 | 1,640.5 / 1,640.6 | 2,057.1 / 2,056.4 |
| tg256 | 100.6 / 100.3 | 99.7 / 100.8 |
| 16K greedy, tokens md5 | 75a302c75b7c | 75a302c75b7c (identical) |

The products use FP16 operands with FP32 sums, so they are not bit-identical to MMQ. The 16K greedy tokens came out identical in all four runs. The same kernel design in a Maya-based engine also matched llama.cpp's greedy output for 128 of 128 tokens on this model.

items.title: cuda: opt-in MMVQ activation reuse across output rows
items.body:
This adds an opt-in exact multi-column MMVQ kernel for Q4_K, Q5_K, Q6_K and IQ4_XS, plus `b6_mmvq_bench`. Each column's Q8_1 activation fragment is loaded once per weight block and reused across multiple output rows. The Q6_K scales remain in registers. The intended arithmetic order matches the existing exact layout.

`STRATA_B6_MMVQ_ROWS=1` selects two output rows per block; `2`, `4`, and `8` select those row counts explicitly. Unset or `0` retains the existing kernel. The new path requires the exact layout, `STRATA_TSUM` off, and a supported format; other calls fall back. The setter/getter are for tools and must be used before graph capture. Single-column calls retain their existing path.

Relationship to current upstream: this branch starts at `82f46a8`. Upstream `d5ea713` now also contains the separate interleaved MMVQ path (`MMVQ_IL`), whose selection is restricted to supported shapes, 2-4 columns, and sm_80 or newer. This PR has not been rebased or measured together with that addition. Its potential relevance includes Turing and calls that use the existing native layout; it should not be described as a measured improvement over the new interleaved path.

Historical evidence, with limits:

- Local fork microbenchmark logs from October 6-7 cover RTX 2080 Ti sm_75 and RTX 3060 sm_86, 15 model-shaped cases, widths 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8. They end with zero failed comparisons for the tested modes. These synthetic checks compare the new and existing exact kernels, and both against individual single-column calls. They are historical fork results, not a fresh test of this PR head.
- In the historical two-row run, for example, GDN qkv Q6_K at four columns was 0.0848 to 0.0654 ms on the 2080 Ti and 0.1372 to 0.1044 ms on the 3060. CUDA-event microbenchmarks do not establish an end-to-end speedup.
- The fork's deterministic full-model runs reported a modest improvement, but forced IDs/windows do not control all cache and speculative work. No causal end-to-end percentage, general quality equivalence, or improvement on latest upstream is claimed here.
- Some wider cases regress; this does not change the default. HIP and other GPU architectures have not been runtime-qualified.

Publication validation:

- Head `8cae814e6e819736e47c95f3b5e8b056c7528c0f`, one commit over `82f46a8c8f475f001ad76d92f58f4a4f8ffb0253`; `git diff --check 82f46a8..HEAD` passes.
- No fresh build or GPU test of this exact branch was performed for publication. Compilation of this exact branch, synthetic parity on both cards, and an integration comparison against current upstream remain pending.

Reproduction after building the CUDA branch:

```text
cmake --build build --target b6_mmvq_bench
build/b6_mmvq_bench 500 -1 1
build/b6_mmvq_bench 500 0 4
```

The first benchmark selects all visible devices and two rows per block; the second selects device 0 and four rows per block. An exit code of zero covers only the benchmark's synthetic case matrix, not full-model equivalence.

items.title: qsa_select: prompt-path block scores with a thread per query head (below sm_80, same bits)
items.body:
## What

The prompt path's QSA block scores on cards without the TF32 scorer (below sm_80; measured on Turing, sm_75) run on a
new kernel that is 4.6-5.2x faster per call, with bitwise the same scores. sm_80 and newer, HIP, and decode run the
same code as before. `STRATA_SCORES_THREAD=0` turns it off.

Two commits:

1. **A thread per (query, head)** (`block_scores_thread_kernel`). The old kernel scored every (query, key block) with
   a whole warp: 20 shuffles and five 512-byte loads per score. Now each lane keeps one 128-value query head in
   registers, reads each key once from shared memory as a broadcast, and adds its 32 four-value partials in the
   same tree that lane 0 of the old xor-shuffle sum used. Same pairs, same order, so the same bits. The heads are
   summed 0..3 from 0.0f as before, and the tail block keeps `block_scores_tail_kernel`.
2. **Four lanes per query.** Nsight Compute showed the first version bound by the shared-memory pipe
   (`mio_throttle`): one key load per 4 FMAs. The old shuffle tree splits into four quarters that only meet at the
   end, so now four lanes share a query, each holds one quarter of all four heads, one key load feeds 16 FMAs, and
   two xor shuffles finish the same tree. Still the same bits.

New test: `qsa_scores_parity` checks every score of the new kernel against `block_scores_kernel` (normal values, wide
magnitudes with zeros, small integers with ties; up to 262K context), then times both.

## Measured

CMP 50HX (TU102, sm_75, unlocked to RTX 2080 speed), CUDA 13.3, GCC 14.2.

- `qsa_scores_parity`: 141 M scores bitwise identical on both cards.
- Time per call, old warp kernel -> this PR:

  | queries | context | before | after |
  |---:|---:|---:|---:|
  | 1,024 | 140K | 35.9 ms | 6.2 ms |
  | 1,024 | 200K | 52.4 ms | 8.5 ms |

- Why it matters: in an nsys profile of one +4.4K-token prompt at 140K (Flash-Next IQ3_XXS, 2x CMP 50HX,
  `--layer-split auto`), `block_scores_kernel` was the largest prompt kernel: 1,045 ms per card, 17 % of the time.
- Whole engine, same setup: a coding-agent session from 34K to 190K tokens (36 turns, +~4.4K tokens each, greedy,
  fresh server per run) gave word-for-word the same text as before. Time to first token at 190K went from 10.49 s to
  7.13 s, but that number also includes the tokenizer change in #1823; the scorer's own share was not split out.

Note: measured on a fork based on 0.1.38. The patch applies to current `main` without changes; re-measuring on 0.1.41
is still to do. Volta and Pascal (the experimental build) also take this kernel and were not tested.

## How to check

On an sm_75 card: `qsa_scores_parity` (also in ctest). It prints `PASS` when every score matches, and the time of both
kernels.

serve: --prompt-cache-spread, checkpoints kept spread back from the conversation's end (opt-in)
items.body:
## What

Opt-in `--prompt-cache-spread`: when the conversation checkpoints are over `--prompt-cache`, the one that leaves is
chosen so that the kept ones stay spread back from the conversation's end, instead of the least recently used. Without
the flag nothing changes.

## Why

The engine keeps 6 checkpoints and rotates them by least recent use. Every turn adds one at its start, so after a few
short turns all of them sit within the last 1-2K tokens (plus the pinned system-prompt root). That is fine while a
client only appends. Agent clients do not always: they trim an old tool output, drop a step, or rewrite an earlier turn
a few thousand tokens back. The new prompt then matches none of the recent checkpoints, the resume falls back to the
system prompt, and the whole conversation is read again.

Found with the pi coding agent (and the pi-blackhole extensions) on a long agent session, from the engine log:

| conversation held | new prompt | same as held for | resumed at | read again |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 210,952 | 210,528 | 204,349 (6K before the end) | 9,525 | 201,003 tokens, 100 s |
| 206,572 | 205,253 | 163,508 (42K before the end) | 0 | 205,253 tokens, 101 s |

In both, a checkpoint a few thousand tokens before the edit would have saved most of the read; least recent use had
rotated those out.

## How

- `conv_cache::spread_victim` (`include/strata/program/conv_cache.hpp`): over the chain (ascending), the victim is the
  checkpoint whose removal leaves the smallest gap for its distance from the newest one,
  `(len[i+1] - len[i-1]) / (len[newest] - len[i-1])`. Dense recent points go first, so the kept ones thin out
  geometrically towards the root. Never the root, the newest or a pinned (`strata_prefix`) one; the
  `--prompt-cache-tail` checkpoint first, as in the existing policy; with no candidate, the existing policy.
- `generate.cpp`: the flag, and the choice between the two policies at the one place a checkpoint is dropped.
- The resume is unchanged: a checkpoint is used only when the prompt starts with exactly its tokens and pictures.
- Same number of checkpoints, no more RAM.

In a simulation of 200 turns of 1,000 tokens after a 9,525-token system prompt (`conv_cache_test`):

| 6 checkpoints, kept (tokens before the end) | edit 6K back | edit 42K back |
|---|---:|---:|
| least recent use: 0, 1K, 2K, 3K, 4K and the root | reads 200K | reads 200K |
| spread: 0, 1K, 3K, 8K, 43K, 200K | reads **8K** | reads **43K** |

## Measured

2x CMP 50HX (Turing sm_75, `--layer-split auto`), 2x Xeon E5-2670 v2, 64 GB RAM, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ3_XXS, CUDA 13.3,
GCC 14. An 82,593-token conversation (a 65K-token document, then 20 short turns sent 2 at a time, each request
continuing the previous one), then the same conversation with a turn ~6 steps back rewritten and a question; greedy,
thinking off:

| | resumed at | time |
|---|---:|---:|
| `--prompt-cache-spread` | 73,610 | **10.2 s** |
| `--prompt-cache 0` (read in full) | 0 | 40.0 s |

With the expert placement fixed (`--adapt-swaps 0 --pcie-frac 0.17`) the answer after the resume was the same text as
the full read. Without fixing it, two full reads already differ in wording (the placement moves with timing), so that
comparison needs the fixed placement.

Tests: `conv_cache_test` passes, with the new cases (the simulation above against least recent use; every candidate
pinned and one slot fall back to the existing policy). Not run on Windows or HIP.

## Relation to #1937

Found while measuring the disk tier of #1937 on the same agent sessions, with a diagnostic that logs how many tokens a
request read again although a held conversation had them. It is independent of #1937: any long conversation whose
client edits its history benefits, with or without parked conversations.

## How to try

Add `"--prompt-cache-spread"` to the config's `args`.

items.title: prompt attention: STRATA_PROMPT_ATTN_IMMA=1 - the int8-KV kernel on INT8 tensor cores (opt-in, closer to FP32)
items.body:
The int8-KV prompt attention (`prompt_attn_i8_kernel`, v2) drifts away from the FP32 kernel on short prompts. On IQ2_XS the first-token KL to the FP32 kernel is 0.025 after a 2K prompt, and the 32 greedy tokens change. This PR adds an opt-in kernel (`STRATA_PROMPT_ATTN_IMMA=1`) that puts both products on INT8 tensor cores with an operand split exact to 24 bits. It is closer to FP64 than v2 at every shape tested and 1.35-1.53x faster per launch. Unset (the default), nothing changes.

### What it does

`prompt_attn_i8v3_kernel` keeps v2's block, its cp.async pipeline and its online softmax.

- **Operands.** QK^T and PV run as `mma m16n8k32` on the int8 K and V codes as stored, with no int8 -> fp16 conversion. The other operand is split into three exact 8-bit parts:
  - q is scaled per (head, 64-dim group) and p·v_scale per (row, chunk), both to 127;
  - then X = rint(x · 65536) = h · 65536 + l · 256 + m, with h and l signed bytes and m an unsigned one (a `u8 x s8` MMA).

  That is 24 bits, finer than v2's FP16 hi + lo split (~22 bits). Each part's int32 sum is exact, and the three parts are combined in FP32.
- **Occupancy.** One K stage and one V stage per warp (K(c+1) is gathered during softmax(c) and PV(c)), 12-row partial sums, and `__launch_bounds__(128, 3)`: ~25.5 KB of shared memory and 168 registers, so 3 blocks per SM instead of v2's 2. The kernel waits on latency, not on its MMAs: with one block per SM it ran 1.54x slower than with two.
- **Scope.** sm_80+ only: the device code is behind the file's `STRATA_PA_SM80`, and Turing / Volta / HIP keep their kernels. The file compiles for 75/80/86/89/120. A test hook, `qsa_prompt_attn_set_imma()`, is added. `qsa_prompt_attn_parity` now checks IMMA against FP64 and v2 and times both.

### Measured

RTX 5090, Ryzen 9 9950X3D, IQ2_XS (ISTA GSQ-RCO), `--kv int8`, `--expert-cache 12000`.

**Kernel accuracy against FP64** (`qsa_prompt_attn_parity`, max relative error, 0 failures):

| context / queries | IMMA | v2 | FP32 kernel |
|---|---|---|---|
| 32K / 2048 | **2.24e-6** | 3.17e-6 | 2.51e-6 |
| 1500 / 1500 | **2.15e-6** | 3.30e-6 | 1.96e-6 |
| 2100 / 256 | **2.64e-6** | 2.78e-6 | 1.90e-6 |

**End to end, first-token KL to the FP32 kernel** (`STRATA_PROMPT_ATTN_OLD=1`); the last column says whether the 32 greedy tokens match the FP32 kernel's:

| prompt | v2 | IMMA | tokens = FP32 (v2 / IMMA) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 600 | 0.0010 | 0.0016 | yes / yes |
| 2K | 0.0248 | **0.0026** | no / **yes** |
| 8K | 0.0009 | 0.0028 | no / **yes** |
| 32K | 0.0340 | **0.0196** | yes / no |

- Median KL: 0.0027 for IMMA against 0.013 for v2.
- The top token is the same everywhere.

items.title: sm_75: a faster tiled FP32 block scorer (STRATA_SELECT_SIMT=2), and the case for SIMT on RTX 20 by default
items.body:
On Turing the prompt path's QSA block scores run the warp kernel (no TF32 tensor cores, so `qsa_block_scores_tc` falls back), and at long context they dominate the prompt. `STRATA_PREFILL_TIMING=1` on an RTX 2080 Ti, appending 16K tokens to a 390K conversation (`--serve`, conversation cache reused):

| phase | default | `STRATA_SELECT_SIMT=1` |
|---|---:|---:|
| qsa select | 19.0 s (61.5 %) | 3.5 s (23.0 %) |
| whole 16K read | 31.5 s (521 tok/s) | 15.9 s (1031 tok/s) |

This PR adds `STRATA_SELECT_SIMT=2`: `block_scores_simt_kernel` with 32 queries × 128 blocks per CTA (8 × 8 products per thread instead of 8 × 4) and the next K chunk's loads in registers while the current one is used. Every (row, block) dot is the same `fmaf` chain over k = 0..127 and the same relu sum over the heads, so its scores are **bitwise those of `=1`**. `qsa_select_bench` gets an optional hash of the fast scorer's bytes (`QSA_BENCH_HASH=1`) to show it: the same hash for `=1` and `=2` at 131K, 262K, 400K and 510K.

`=2` stays opt-in like `=1`. The second half of this description is the data I'd offer for turning SIMT on by default on sm_75 (your call, as with `STRATA_BF16_TC`).

## Setup

RTX 2080 Ti 22 GB (sm_75, PCIe 3.0 x16), i7-6700, 56 GB DDR4-2133, CUDA 13.0, driver 595, SM clock locked at 1650 MHz, 240 W. `v0.1.43` built from source with `-DSTRATA_BUILD_TESTS=ON`. Model Q2_0, `--resident-experts`, `--spec 4 --spec-min-p 0.7`, `--max-context 524288` (YaRN ×2), `--kv int8 --kv-resident 32768`.

## Scorer: `qsa_select_bench CTX 256 5 524288`

| context | warp kernel | SIMT=1 | SIMT=2 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 131K | 7.66 ms | 1.21 ms | 0.95 ms |
| 262K | 15.25 ms | 2.01 ms | 1.87 ms |
| 400K | 23.24 ms | 2.96 ms | 2.82 ms |
| 510K | 29.60 ms | 3.77 ms | 3.57 ms |

Selections against the warp kernel: 256/256 identical at 262K, 400K and 510K, 255/256 at 131K (0.0002 % of cells). Accuracy against FP64: max error 5.8e-5 vs the warp kernel's 2.1e-5 (2.3e-7 of the score scale).

## Engine, one-shot, `STRATA_SELECT_SIMT` 0 vs 2

Prompt read, same binary, real text (the 256K token file of the benches):

| prompt | default | SIMT=2 | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 49K | 1349 tok/s | 1451 | +7.6 % |
| 98K | 1230 | 1434 | +16.6 % |
| 147K | 1129 | 1407 | +24.6 % |
| 197K | 1042 | 1380 | +32.4 % |

The method from #655 (docs/UNSLOTH_Q4.md): a `--serve` engine with `--adapt-every 100000`, the first P tokens read by the prompt path (the path this changes) as one request, then the next 2,048 tokens resumed at P through the verify windows with `--short-read`, `STRATA_LOGPOS` with `STRATA_LOGPOS_TOPK=20` writing every position. Raw text (Don Quixote, Spanish).

| prefix read batched | positions | argmax agreement | KL (off ‖ on) | perplexity off / on | argmax where off's top-2 gap ≥ 0.5 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32,768 | 2,047 | 97.9 % | 0.0099 | 4.552 / 4.620 | 1954 / 1970 |
| 98,304 | 2,047 | 95.3 % | 0.0136 | 5.409 / 5.416 | 1672 / 1686 |

items.title: CUDA prefill VRAM loans and SM75 Q4/native-IQ opt-ins
items.body:
# CUDA prefill VRAM loans and SM75 Q4/native-IQ opt-ins

tldr; massive PP speed win on my 8GB VRAM laptop GPU

## Summary

This branch adds two manual Turing prompt-compute paths and one manual,
request-scoped CUDA memory feature:

1. An SM75 Q4 prompt-attention tensor-core path, selected with
   `STRATA_PROMPT_ATTN_Q4_TC=1` and compiled with the qualified 64-cell tile.
2. A native IQ expert path for supported IQ3/IQ4 expert formats, selected with
   `STRATA_PF_FUSED_NATIVE_SM75=1`. The separately manual
   `STRATA_PF_FUSED_NATIVE_SM75_ADAPTIVE=1` enables the per-format SM75 shape
   probe; unsupported layers remain on the existing path.
3. Request-scoped VRAM loans for the serialized, single-NVIDIA-GPU server path.
   They temporarily use decode-only VRAM for the expert cache during prefill,
   then restore the verifier, native head and MTP resources before generation.
   A repeat-prefill option applies the same transaction to later long messages.

The Q4-attention and native-IQ paths are SM75-specific. The VRAM-loan feature
does not require SM75: it can apply to other NVIDIA CUDA GPUs with virtual
memory management and the supported single-GPU server configuration. The
compute-path measurements below use an RTX 2080 Super Max-Q; the loan is also
qualified separately on an RTX 4070 Ti.

All switches are off when absent. Existing behavior is therefore unchanged for
users who do not opt in.

## Benchmark platform

- GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Super Max-Q, 8 GiB, 105 W limit, SM75
- CPU/RAM: Intel i7-10875H, 64 GiB RAM
- PCIe: PCIe 3.0 x16; measured host-to-device bandwidth about 12.2 GB/s
- OS/build: Windows, CUDA 13.4, MSVC, Release build with SM75 SASS
- Model: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ3_XXS, native GGUF plus IQ3_XXS expert pack
- Context: 65,536 tokens
- MTP: enabled, `--spec 4`, same draft model and profile in each matched arm
- Speed projection: enabled and held constant
- Sampling: temperature 0 for benchmark requests
- PP/TG are the engine-reported rates from the timing line.

The long-prompt qualification used approximately 31,258 fresh prompt tokens
and a 512-token completion cap. Each run was serialized, started with a fresh
engine, and checked for normal completion. No parallel Strata servers were
used.

## Results

### End-to-end results

Each row is the median of three fresh-engine runs over 31,258 prompt tokens and
512 generated tokens. Baseline and opt-in runs use the same v0.1.41 source
revision, model, prompt and runtime settings.

| KV | Build | Prompt plan | PP (tok/s) | TG (tok/s) | PP range |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Q4_0 | Feature flags off | 2,304 / 227 | 422.5 | 23.4 | 422.4--424.4 |
| Q4_0 | All applicable opt-ins | 4,864 / 512 | **865.2** | **23.6** | 863.5--881.0 |
| INT8 | Feature flags off | 1,792 / 227 | 435.8 | 22.9 | 435.6--436.1 |
| INT8 | Native IQ and loans | 4,352 / 512 | **854.7** | **21.2** | 849.3--865.5 |

The Q4_0 result is **+104.8% PP** with effectively unchanged TG. The INT8
result is **+96.1% PP** and **-7.4% TG**; its TG range was 21.1--23.1 and stayed
within the 10% guardrail. These are complete-stack results, not percentages for
individual features: the opt-ins also change prompt chunk, staging-ring and
expert-cache geometry.

The Q4_0 opt-in runs used:

```json
{
  "STRATA_BF16_TC": "1",
  "STRATA_PROMPT_ATTN_Q4_TC": "1",
  "STRATA_PF_FUSED": "1",
  "STRATA_PF_FUSED_NATIVE": "1",
  "STRATA_PF_FUSED_NATIVE_SM75": "1",
  "STRATA_PF_FUSED_NATIVE_SM75_ADAPTIVE": "1",
  "STRATA_PREFILL_ELASTIC_LOAN": "1",
  "STRATA_PREFILL_MTP_LOAN": "1",
  "STRATA_PREFILL_HEAD_LOAN": "1",
  "STRATA_PREFILL_RETAIN_STARTUP_CHUNK": "1",
  "STRATA_SELECT_SIMT": "1"
}
```

`STRATA_PREFILL_REPEAT_LOAN=1` is used only for the subsequent-message
qualification below; it does not participate in a fresh engine's first prompt.
For subsequent messages, `STRATA_PREFILL_REPEAT_MIN_TOKENS` sets the minimum
number of uncached prompt tokens that triggers releasing and reloading the
decode-only resources. It defaults to `1024` and is clamped to a minimum of
`256`. The threshold does not govern the first prompt: the startup MTP/head
loan is an engine-start on/off choice because those resources are deferred
before the first request length is known.

### Individual feature evidence

- **SM75 Q4 prompt attention:** with native IQ, loans and the 4,864/512 plan
  held constant, enabling only this path changed the three-run median from
  613.6 to 849.8 PP (**+38.5%**). QSA attention fell from about 19.2 to 5.1
  seconds.
- **SM75 native IQ:** the matched native-off median was 749.1 PP; the fixed
  native path measured 829.4 PP (**+10.7%**). This comparison also changed the
  plan from 5,376/227 to 4,864/512, so it is not a pure kernel-only percentage.
- **Prompt VRAM loans:** there is no clean three-run, same-planner loan-only
  comparison, so this PR does not assign the loan a percentage. Its observable
  effect is enabling the larger cache/chunk geometry and restoring all deferred
  decode resources before generation.

The existing `STRATA_SELECT_SIMT=1` option can compound with these changes: an
exact full-stack A/B changed 849.8 to 879.9 PP (**+3.54%**). SIMT is not part of
this PR.

### Subsequent-message loan

One serialized-session qualification used INT8 KV, a 131,072-token context and
128-MiB VRAM segments. After a 60-token warm-up, a 32,458-token
subsequent prompt selected 3,328/512 and completed at **787.0 PP / 23.1 TG**
with 512 generated tokens. The request released and restored the verifier,
native output head, MTP experts and draft head without a CUDA/runtime error.

For example, a configuration that only takes repeat loans when at least 50,000
new prompt tokens remain after prompt-cache reuse can use:

```json
{
  "STRATA_PREFILL_ELASTIC_LOAN": "1",
  "STRATA_PREFILL_MTP_LOAN": "1",
  "STRATA_PREFILL_HEAD_LOAN": "1",
  "STRATA_PREFILL_REPEAT_LOAN": "1",
  "STRATA_PREFILL_REPEAT_MIN_TOKENS": "50000"
}
```

### Cross-GPU VRAM-loan qualification

The loan is not SM75-specific. A separate test used an RTX 4070 Ti
(12 GiB, SM89), INT8 KV, a 196,608-token context, a 512-slot staging ring and
the same v0.1.41 source revision. Loan-off and loan-on runs were interleaved,
serialized, and started from a fresh engine. The 36k result is a three-run
median and the 72k result is a five-run median; both used a 512-token
completion cap.

| Fresh prompt | Loan | Prompt chunk | PP (tok/s) | TG (tok/s) | GPU prefill |
| ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 36,061 tokens | Off | 8,448--8,960 | **2,562.9** | **54.8** | 13.811 s |
| 36,061 tokens | On | 15,104 | 2,539.4 | 52.9 | **12.987 s** |
| 72,061 tokens | Off | 8,960 | 2,617.0 | 54.1 | 27.271 s |
| 72,061 tokens | On | 15,104 | **2,680.9** | **54.9** | **25.772 s** |

The larger loan-backed chunk reduced median GPU prompt work by 6.0% at 36k
tokens and 5.5% at 72k. Loading the deferred output-head and MTP resources is
a fixed boundary cost, so the 36k request was 0.9% slower by the engine's
end-to-end PP rate while the 72k request was 2.4% faster. The five-run 72k PP
ranges were 2,604.3--2,633.7 off and 2,501.1--2,696.3 on; four of five loan-on
runs were 2,673.5 PP or higher, with one retained slow outlier. This is evidence
that the general CUDA loan works beyond Turing, but also that it should remain a
manual opt-in: benefit depends on prompt length and whether the released VRAM
crosses a useful planner threshold.

## Correctness and safety

- Default behavior is unchanged; all three families are manual opt-ins.
- The Q4 attention change is prompt-only.
- `STRATA_SELECT_SIMT=1` is also prompt-only, but uses a different FP32 tiled
  scorer and summation order; it can change selected cells and reasoning text.
- Native IQ dispatch is prompt-only and only supported formats use the native
  kernel; unsupported formats fall back to MMQ/previous behavior.
- Routing IDs, expert selection, route weights, and scatter order are not
  changed by these features.
- The loan path is NVIDIA CUDA-specific but not SM75-specific. It requires
  `--serve`, `--vram-elastic`, CUDA virtual memory management, one GPU and a
  VRAM segment of at least 64 MiB.
- The loan path is rejected for batch/shared sessions, pipeline windows,
  layer-split or multi-GPU configurations, helper caches, peer-device mode and
  HIP.
- Deferred verifier reload reapplies request sampling and token history.
- Native-IQ parity checks passed on the RTX 2080. Q4 prompt-attention parity
  passed at 4,096/512 and 1,500/512. The native
  IQ3_XXS/IQ4_NL test retained a fused-vs-rounded RMS of `4.811e-05`. The
  focused validation set passed 10/10, and the Release SM75 build completed
  without an error.
- A repeat-prefill request released and restored the verifier,
  native head, MTP routed experts and draft head, then completed 512 generated
  tokens without a CUDA/runtime error.
- A bounded visible-answer capture completed normally; the matched quality
  capture for native shape selection had identical bounded reasoning and draft
  acceptance. A separate SIMT quality pair returned the same visible control
  line and normal stop, but reasoning differed, as expected from the changed
  scorer arithmetic. A full unrestricted answer-parity sweep remains future
  work.

items.body:
Title:
fused_gr: TILE=1280 kernel specialization for sm_75 (Turing) down-projection

Body:

## What this does

On Turing (sm_75) the fused gate/rescale down-projection kernel runs with
the default tile geometry sized for larger shared-memory budgets. Turing
has 64 KiB of shared memory per block (opt-in), which fits a different,
more efficient shape: a TILE=1280 specialization fits **8 activation
tokens in a single ~40 KiB launch** instead of the default tile's
smaller working set, and drops register pressure (REG 76 → 64) enough to
raise occupancy.

- Adds a `sm_75`-guarded TILE=1280 instantiation of the down-projection
  kernel alongside the default geometry.
- Bit-exact: the kernel still accumulates in strictly increasing
  (tile, chunk) order, so results are unchanged — verified greedy
  generation matches the default build with temperature 0.
- No effect on other architectures (guarded, default path untouched).

## Measured on my machine

i7-8700K (AVX2), RTX 2070 (sm_75), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next native Q2_0 pack
(spec verified from the GGUF header, ~125.7B-parameter MoE), standalone
kernel microbench, temperature 0.

- Kernel level (verify-window timing of the down-projection launches,
  stage profiler on):
  - GDN down: **2.73–2.80 → 1.88–1.98 ms/window (−30 %)**
  - QSA down: **0.90–0.93 → 0.62–0.65 ms/window (−30 %)**
- End to end on this rig: within noise, **because decode is CPU
  expert-pool bound here** (the CPU AVX2 expert pool dominates the
  window). This change frees GPU time the CPU cannot consume yet, so its
  end-to-end benefit should appear on rigs with a faster CPU or a larger
  model where the GPU down-projection is the bottleneck.
- Profiling context (Nsight Compute, verify-window kernel capture): the
  grouped-expert kernels on sm_75 are L1TEX-pipe bound (~95 % of peak,
  DRAM ~22–33 %), driven by uncoalesced 8-byte weight reads. The tile
  change improves occupancy and per-launch batching without touching the
  access pattern or the summation order.

## Please test on other devices

I can only measure one machine. This is a Turing-specific specialization,
so other sm_75 cards (RTX 2060/2070/2080 variants) are the direct target:

- **RTX 20-series owners**: please rerun a fixed-prompt greedy decode
  (temperature 0) before/after and compare wall-clock decode time, and
  ideally per-window kernel time if you use the stage profiler.
- **Non-Turing GPUs** should be unaffected (guard), but confirmation is
  welcome — especially Ampere+ cards with the larger default smem budget,
  to confirm the default path is untouched.
- Rigs with fast CPUs (where GPU decode share is larger) are where the
  end-to-end effect should actually show.

Greedy outputs should be identical before/after; if you see a difference,
that's a bug, please report it.

items.title: qsa_prompt_attn: Volta (sm_70) crashes in the prompt path - compare the full compute capability
items.body:
## The bug

With 0.1.31 built for a V100 (`-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=70 -DSTRATA_EXPERIMENTAL_SM60=ON`), the engine loads and
answers a 22-token prompt, then dies on the first ~900-token prompt:

```
prefill copy_i32: unspecified launch failure
```

`qsa_prompt_attn_batch` reads only the compute capability's major version: `< 7` refuses the device, `< 8` means
Turing. A V100 is 7.0, so it passes as Turing and launches the m16n8k8 kernel. In a sm_70 build `mma16816` compiles that
kernel to `__trap()` (`__CUDA_ARCH__ < 750`), and the trap surfaces at the next sync as the launch failure above. The
comment above the check already says an older card should keep the old kernel; only the check missed Volta.

## The fix

Compare major*10+minor: below 75 returns false (the old kernel), below 80 is Turing. The variable is renamed from
`cc_major` to `cc` because it now holds both parts. No change for sm_75 and newer, AMD, or Pascal (6.x was already
refused).

## Tested

Tesla V100-PCIE-16GB, CUDA 12.4, Linux, IQ3_S pack, `--kv int8 --spec 4`, greedy, 256 tokens out:

| Prompt | Before | After (prompt / output tok/s) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 22 tokens | OK | OK |
| ~900 tokens | crash | 222 / 40 |
| ~6.8K tokens | crash | 680 / 41.5 |
| ~26.7K tokens | crash | 966 / 43 |

These match 0.1.26 on the same card (221 / 680 / 982 tok/s prompt). The UD-Q4_K_XL import also runs with the fix
(~20 tok/s output, with every expert in RAM).

items.title: prefill: opt-in STRATA_HC_UPMIX=1 on CUDA - the hyper-connection up projection with gr_mix_r as its epilogue (sm_80+)
items.body:
`STRATA_HC_UPMIX=1` (31b2472a) fuses the hyper-connection read's up projection with `gr_mix_r` on gfx11; on CUDA `gr_upmix` returns false and the pair runs. This adds a CUDA kernel (sm_80+) behind the same switch.

Unset (the default), nothing changes: no new code runs, and the output is byte-identical to v0.1.40.2.

### Why

Each layer half's read runs the up GEMM, which writes `gated` (T x 10240 FP32, 336 MB for an 8,192-token chunk). `gr_mix_r` then reads it back with R. `gr_mix_r` already runs at ~96% of the bandwidth (102 KB per token in 0.489 ms at 8K on an RTX 5090), so only fewer bytes make the read faster. Fused, `gated` is never written or read.

### What it does

- **The kernel.** `gr_upmix_cuda_kernel` computes a block of 128 tokens x 32 columns x the 4 streams.
  - K = 320 is staged in 32-deep slices (`cp.async`, double-buffered).
  - 8 warps run `mma.m16n8k16` BF16 with FP32 accumulation (`ldmatrix`).
  - A lane ends with its (token, column) pairs for all 4 streams, so the mix runs in registers, in `gr_mix_r_kernel`'s order, and writes `mixed` with its BF16 / FP16 images.
  - The epilogue's R rows are prefetched into L2 when the block starts. The grid is column-tile fastest, as on gfx11.
- **Where it runs.** On sm_80+ (`cp.async` and the BF16 `mma`), checked per device; `STRATA_EMULATE_CC` is honoured. On Turing, `gr_upmix` returns false and the pair runs. On CUDA, chunks under 33 tokens also keep the pair (see the parity results below).
- **Not changed.** The gfx11 kernel, HIP and SYCL; `gr_upmix`'s signature; `STRATA_HC_UPMIX_CHECK`.
- **Test.** `gr_upmix_parity` (ctest; GPU, synthetic, no model) compares the fused read with cuBLAS + `gr_mix_r` and with FP64. `--bench` adds timings.

### Measured

RTX 5090, CUDA 13.3, Windows.

**Parity** (`gr_upmix_parity`, 21 sizes from 1 to 32,768 tokens, 0 failures):

- **From 33 tokens up, bitwise.** `mixed`, the BF16 image and the FP16 image all equal the pair's. cuBLAS's up GEMM sums K in the kernel's order at these sizes.
- **Below 33 tokens, rounding-level.** cuBLAS picks another kernel there: `mixed` max |diff| / max |value| is at most 1.8e-7, and at most 0.010% of the BF16 and 0.058% of the FP16 values differ. Both paths are equally close to FP64. These chunks keep the pair anyway.

**Kernel** (`--bench`, medians of 20 alternating runs, ms):

| T | up GEMM + `gr_mix_r` | fused | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2,048 | 0.100 + 0.101 = 0.201 | 0.141 | 1.42x |
| 8,192 | 0.338 + 0.489 = 0.828 | 0.458 | 1.81x |
| 32,768 | 1.814 + 4.103 = 5.919 | 2.707 | 2.19x |

**Prompt** (IQ2_XS, `generate`, `--prefill auto`, 3 interleaved pairs, ms; "hc read" is `STRATA_PREFILL_TIMING`'s phase):

| prompt | off: prompt / hc read | `=1`: prompt / hc read |
|---|---|---|
| 2,099 tokens | 1,004 / 114, 901 / 103, 896 / 104 | 955 / 101, 863 / 97, 898 / 102 |
| 8,034 tokens | 1,646 / 202, 1,713 / 206, 1,726 / 210 | 1,571 / 164, 1,697 / 166, 1,637 / 173 |
| 32,036 tokens (4 chunks) | 5,968 / 567, 6,012 / 575, 5,874 / 549 | 5,752 / 429, 5,736 / 431, 5,519 / 407 |

The hc read takes 19% less time at 8K and 24% less at 32K, which makes the prompt 4% faster. At 2K the read is a small share of the prompt and the difference is within the noise.

**Identity** (IQ2_XS, first-token logits and 32 greedy tokens against v0.1.40.2's engine, same expert cache):

- **Unset.** Identical after 600, 2K and 32K tokens.
- **`=1`.** The logits are identical at all three lengths, and so are the tokens at 600 and 2K. `STRATA_HC_UPMIX_CHECK=100000` found every fused read of the 32K prompt bitwise equal to the pair (all 384 of them, 4 chunks).
- **The 32K tokens with `=1`.** They differ, but not because of the numbers.
  - The suffix-draft policy (#1252) learns from measured time, so a faster prompt changes which drafts it tries and how the verify windows are batched. The log shows 2 suffix-draft windows (2 of 3 drafts accepted) instead of 4 (6 of 9).
  - With `--suffix-draft 0`, both engines give the same 32 tokens.
  - That is why the switch stays opt-in on CUDA too.

**Builds.** `75-real;75-virtual;86-real;89-real;120a-real` (the release list plus sm_75 PTX) builds `strata` and the test. `gr_upmix_parity` and `gemm_bf16_parity` pass. The kernel ran only on sm_120; the bitwise result is cuBLAS 13.3's on that card.

## What this does

`mma.m16n8k16` (f16) needs sm_80, so main compiles the tensor-core prompt attention to a trap on sm_75 and those cards run the fp32-FMA kernel — the gap #87 left in ("the sm_80 guard on the tensor-core prompt attention"). Turing (sm_75) has `mma.m16n8k8` with the **same A/B/C register mapping**, so each k=16 step becomes two k=8 steps on the fragments exactly as they are already laid out (a[0]/a[1] with b[0], a[2]/a[3] with b[1]). The sum rounds twice, so the two paths do not agree bit for bit. Turing therefore takes the v1 kernel, which has no cp.async dependency.

## Measured (Quadro RTX 8000, CUDA 12.9, arch 75)

- `qsa_prompt_attn_parity` (`-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=75`): **PASS, FAILURES: 0**; vs FP64 new 6.99e-06, old 2.37e-06 (output scale 3.62); int8 kernel 62.3 → 19.6 ms per chunk (**3.19x**), fp16 65.0 → 25.1 ms (2.59x)
- Engine, three Turing cards (RTX 8000 + 2× RTX 6000), on 0.1.29 main: 9.7K-token prompt **1,050 → 1,177 tok/s**, 41.7K **1,124 → 1,251 tok/s**; an 80K needle test answers correctly
- Single-card relevance: #139's thread measured main 0.1.27 at PP 731-738 tok/s on one RTX 2080 Ti — this kernel is that card's prompt path too

Developed with Claude Code (GLM-5.3-Flash): implementation, sm_75 parity runs and the measurements above.

i got the experimental sm_70 build running on my Tesla V100 32GB (IQ2_XS) and found two things that were slow there, so here are fixes for both. i know volta isn't supported, this just makes the existing experimental build faster

it's the V100 build you mentioned in #101 / #130

1. **BF16 GEMMs on volta and turing.** these cards have no BF16 tensor cores, so cuBLAS runs them as a CUDA-core kernel (`magma_sgemmEx`), about 10% of the GPU time in a prompt on a V100. on cc 7.0 and 7.5 i now convert the operands to FP16 in the existing scratch buffer and use the FP16 tensor-core path. `STRATA_BF16_VIA_F16=0` turns it off

(#600 adds a tensor-core prompt attention for sm_70, which would take over prefill there. this kernel still runs decode and the verify windows, and the two PRs share no files)

### numbers

V100, prompt processing speed, v0.1.37, one run each, `--kv int8`:

| prompt | upstream | + attention fix | + attention and BF16 fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8K tokens | 874 tok/s | 934 (+7%) | 1066 (+22%) |
| 20K tokens | 896 tok/s | 960 (+7%) | 1100 (+23%) |

| prompt | off | on |
|---|---|---|
| 3.7K tokens | 131.1 tok/s | 141.8 (+8%) |
| 7.2K tokens | 137.0 tok/s | 149.5 (+9%) |

the attention commit alone gives byte-identical first-window logits to upstream at 8K and 20K.

the BF16 one is not bit-identical, since FP16 accumulation rounds differently and tiny values lose precision. i compared 24 different slices of source code, 1.5K to 5.5K tokens each, and the next-token distribution after prefill: mean KL 8.4e-3, max 3.7e-2, same top-1 in 23 of 24 (the odd one is a near tie), and perplexity of the true next token 3.448 vs 3.420, so no measurable change. that's source code only, on the V100, and only right after the prompt, not a long generation. the BF16X2 remainder GEMMs stay on cuBLAS because their values are too small for FP16
